ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Before the experiment, all participants affirmed their consent to participate in the study and provided written consent in accordance with ethical procedures approved by the Bioethics Committee of [BLINDED FOR REVIEW].
We recruited 484 participants (331 females) via internal email and social networking.
Participants were from Colombia (41.1%) and Peru (58.9%).
First, participants were exposed to faces of political candidates under time constraints (speeded block), and asked to rate their feelings of honesty and competence.
Second, participants were asked to rate the likelihood of choosing each political candidate for a public position.
Participants were asked to respond quickly, using their first instinct.
Once the scale disappeared, participants were asked if they recognized the target face through a yes/no recognition judgment.

Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

text.text: Rapid judgments based on political candidates' facial features often predict electoral outcomes.
Building on this, we explored how facial impressions of honesty and competence-formed under suboptimal processing conditions-predict voting intentions for actual political candidates.
In this study, 484 participants (Colombians: 199; Peruvians: 285; male: 30.2%) were exposed to candidate faces from Colombia and Peru under time constraints (33 ms or 100 ms).
Participants rated these faces on honesty and competence and subsequently indicated their likelihood of voting for each candidate.

Our findings demonstrate that while rapid facial impressions predict voting preferences overall, this effect is strongly amplified when candidates are recognized from one's own country, whereas for foreign candidates, the relationship remains minimal or disappears.
Crucially, because voting intentions were evaluated during subsequent unconstrained viewing, these rapid impressions interact with fullviewing processing rather than acting in complete isolation.

By utilizing real candidate photographs, this study confirms that rapid facial impressions align with electoral preferences in naturalistic settings, operating through an integrated process where familiar faces instantly retrieve pre-existing political attitudes.
The inherent complexity of voting frequently prompts voters to employ cognitive heuristics to facilitate their choices.
Empirical research consistently demonstrates that voters frequently rely on candidate appearance during the electoral process (Ahler et al., 2017; Olivola & Todorov, 2010).
text.formatted: Empirical research consistently demonstrates that voters frequently rely on candidate appearance during the electoral process <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ahler et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Olivola & Todorov, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This phenomenon has been interpreted by some as an indication of voter irrationality or a lack of information (Banducci et al., 2008; Lenz & Lawson, 2011).
text.formatted: This phenomenon has been interpreted by some as an indication of voter irrationality or a lack of information <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Banducci et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lenz & Lawson, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The present research addresses the influence of facial impressions on voting intention by exploring how facial impressions of honesty and competence made under suboptimal processing conditions predict voting intention of real political candidates.
We chose to situate the research within the electoral contexts of Colombia and Peru, given the situation that both countries held presidential elections in 2026.
For this reason, it is a rare opportunity to study the automatic component of electoral preferences in real-world contexts.
The human face constitutes a special stimulus category within the visual recognition system, processed distinctly from other types of stimuli (Farah et al., 1995; Tsao et al., 2008).
text.formatted: The human face constitutes a special stimulus category within the visual recognition system, processed distinctly from other types of stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Farah et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Tsao et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: This distinct processing is characterized by holistic recognition (Richler, et al., 2011) and a tendency to easily grab attention (Young & Bruce, 2023).
text.formatted: This distinct processing is characterized by holistic recognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Richler, et al., 2011)</ref> and a tendency to easily grab attention <ref type="bibr">(Young & Bruce, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Facial features shape evaluations in several domains.
People rely on faces when making social judgments because the face is a readily accessible type of stimuli (Hahn et al., 2018; Jaeger et al., 2019a).
text.formatted: People rely on faces when making social judgments because the face is a readily accessible type of stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hahn et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Jaeger et al., 2019a)</ref>.

text.text: This sensitivity may be rooted in innate predispositions, which are placed even during intrauterine life (Ronga et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This sensitivity may be rooted in innate predispositions, which are placed even during intrauterine life <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Ronga et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Further, facial features are often believed to be a reliable source of social information (Jaeger et al., 2019b), even when their diagnostic validity is controversial (Jaeger et al., 2024; Giacomin & Rule, 2019; Holtzman, 2011; Todorov et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Further, facial features are often believed to be a reliable source of social information <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Jaeger et al., 2019b)</ref>, even when their diagnostic validity is controversial <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Jaeger et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Giacomin & Rule, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Holtzman, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Todorov et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: There is a consistent positive bias regarding attractive faces (Langlois et al., 2000; Olivera-La Rosa et al., 2025), which has been explained as a "halo effect" (Kahneman, 2011), in which the salient features of the stimuli shape global inferences that are consistent with the evaluation of the face.

text.text: From an evolutionary perspective, making extremely quick judgments based on facial features may constitute a highly adaptive cognitive tool for reducing undesired social interactions, since the cost of acting quickly and making a mistake is lower than the cost of conducting a thorough analysis of the person before acting (Schaller & Park, 2011).

text.text: Recent adversarial collaboration on social evaluation suggests that social perception is dealt using two main dimensions: Horizontal (i.e., to what extent the target is willing and able to create positive social relations with others) and Vertical (i.e., to what extent the target is willing and able to achieve their personal intentions whatever those may be).
Further, each dimension is divided into two facets: Morality and Friendliness compose the Horizontal dimension and Ability and Assertiveness compose the Vertical one (Abele et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Further, each dimension is divided into two facets: Morality and Friendliness compose the Horizontal dimension and Ability and Assertiveness compose the Vertical one <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abele et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Extensive research shows that these two dimensions (also referred as Warmth and Competence, Fiske et al., 2007) guide impression formation across social contexts and predict affective, cognitive, and behavioral responses to others (Luna-Cortes, 2025).
text.formatted: Extensive research shows that these two dimensions (also referred as Warmth and Competence, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Fiske et al., 2007)</ref> guide impression formation across social contexts and predict affective, cognitive, and behavioral responses to others <ref type="bibr">(Luna-Cortes, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This theory has been widely applied to appearance-based judgments, showing that warmth and competence can be rapidly inferred from faces alone.
Facial features automatically activate stereotypes associated with these dimensions, even in the absence of conscious deliberation (Imhoff et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Facial features automatically activate stereotypes associated with these dimensions, even in the absence of conscious deliberation <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Imhoff et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Such inferences are consequential: warmth-related impressions are closely linked to trust, moral evaluation, and humanization, whereas competence is associated with perceived status, leadership ability, and effectiveness (Luna-Cortes, 2025).

In the political domain, prior research based on social evaluation indicates that voters infer candidates' friendliness and competence from appearance and use these impressions to guide voting intentions, particularly when political knowledge or familiarity with the candidate is low (Fiske, 2019; Unkelbach et al., 2023).

text.text: Specifically, there is a consistent positive bias towards perceived facial competence in voting behavior (Ballew & Todorov, 2007; Hall et al., 2009; Laustsen & Petersen, 2018; Todorov et al., 2005).

text.text: Effects of first impressions from faces may be sensitive to cultural differences and political orientation.

Greater perceived power (dominance and facial maturity) in a candidates' face predicted US electoral success, whereas greater perceived warmth (likability and trustworthiness) predicted Japanese voters (Rule et al., 2010).

text.text: Right-wing and conservative candidates are more likely to be voted when their faces look dominant, while liberals' candidates are more likely to lose votes when they are perceived as dominant (Laustsen & Petersen, 2015 , 2016), suggesting that political leanings may moderate the impact of inferences based on facial features.

text.text: While competence has often been highlighted as a predictor of electoral success, the moral primacy hypothesis of social evaluation suggests that moralityrelated judgments (i.e., those linked to honesty and corruption) may emerge earlier in the perceptual process and exert a stronger influence under conditions of uncertainty.

Individuals are motivated to first assess whether another person poses a potential threat or benefit, before evaluating their capacity to enact those intentions (Fiske et al., 2007 , Leach et al., 2007; Brambilla et al., 2012).

text.text: Research on the time course of face processing has shown that people extract information about a face very rapidly (Bar et al., 2006 , Dobs et al., 2019). Willis and Todorov (2006) showed that trustworthiness judgments from facial features are consistently made after 100ms exposure to novel faces, and that these judgments can even be made as little as 33 ms (Todorov et al., 2009).

text.text: Because deciding whether an unfamiliar person is trustworthy is critical in social settings, the efficiency of these trustworthiness judgments is likely due to their adaptive value (Engell et al., 2007). text.text: Based on the reviewed literature, it remains an empirical question whether evaluative judgments, such as trustworthiness, occur before the processing of more detailed, specific facial information, such as identity information or other social evaluation processes such as competence evaluation.

Furthermore, more research is needed to determine whether judgments of trustworthiness and competence derived from facial appearance can occur at early stages of facial processing in the electoral context.

Building on previous research showing that perceived trustworthiness and perceived competence are crucial traits in person perception (Fiske et al., 2007), and that the perception of these traits shapes voters' preferences when choosing which candidate to elect (Laustsen & Petersen, 2018; Olivola & Todorov, 2010; Rule et al., 2010), we explored whether quick first impressions have predictive value for electoral preferences.

text.text: Specifically, we assess whether Colombians and Peruvians judge political candidates' honesty and competence just by seeing their faces under suboptimal processing conditions, and how these impressions predict voting intentions.
The following hypotheses are examined: -H1: When a candidate is unknown, facial impressions of honesty and competence made under suboptimal processing conditions predict voting intention.
Whereas they will not predict voting intention when the candidate is previously known.

A significant main effect with faster RTs for honesty would support H2) and H3 (Within honesty trials, RTs for the evaluative judgment and the recognition judgment will be compared using judgment type as the key predictor) were untestable with the collected dataset.

Hence, we re-phrased them as Exploratory Research Questions: RQ1: Is the correlation between honesty impressions and voting intentions stronger than correlation between competence and voting intentions?
RQ2a:Is the relation between competence impressions and voting intentions more strongly affected by exposure duration than the relation between honesty impressions and voting intentions?

Based on the moral primacy account, we expected the honesty-vote relation to remain largely stable across exposure durations, because honesty-relevant information is extracted early in face processing, whereas the competence-vote relation was expected to strengthen with increasing processing time.
RQ2b: Is the relation between candidate identity and voting intentions more strongly affected by exposure duration than the relation between honesty impressions and voting intentions?

text.text: We recruited 484 participants (331 females) via internal email and social networking.
Participants were from Colombia (41.1%) and Peru (58.9%).
By using samples from both countries, each population serves as a preliminary familiarity control sample for the other country.
We assumed that Colombian candidates would not be familiar to the Peruvian population, and vice versa.

Before the experiment, all participants affirmed their consent to participate in the study and provided written consent in accordance with ethical procedures approved by the Bioethics Committee of [BLINDED FOR REVIEW].
They then indicated their age, gender, educational level and country of residence.
The experimental design consisted of two parts.
First, participants were exposed to faces of political candidates under time constraints (speeded block), and asked to rate their feelings of honesty and competence.

We tested our hypotheses by using a 2x2x2x2 mixed factorial design, with candidates (Colombia/Peru), exposure times (33/100 ms) and evaluative judgment (Honesty/Competence) as within subjects factors, and participants residence (Colombia/Peru) as between subject factor.
Second, participants were asked to rate the likelihood of choosing each political candidate for a public position.

Notably, because voting intentions were evaluated during this subsequent unconstrained viewing phase, the design assesses how initial speeded impressions inform and interact with post-exposure evaluative decisions, rather than measuring voting choices strictly under continuous suboptimal conditions.
40 faces of political candidates to the presidential election of Colombia (20) and Peru (20) were selected as target faces.
We use real pictures of political candidates in both Colombian and Peruvian presidential elections to increase the ecological value of this research.

Although using real public pictures implies an inherent variability in dimensions crucial to social perception such as attractiveness or age (among others), we believe that our approach is best suited to understand how snap judgments from facial information shape voting intentions in real electoral contexts.
To mitigate this methodological issue, we established two methodological controls.

First, target faces were selected from the Internet following defined criteria: a) The 20 most popular candidates from each country were selected, b) Official photos or photos taken intentionally for electoral purposes (not candid photos), c) All photos depict faces clearly visible, d) Faces with neutral to positive emotional expressions were considered, photos with extreme emotional expressions (e.g., exaggerated smiles) were excluded.
An oval shape was applied to all faces to prevent the background from providing additional information (see supplementary material).

Second, a pilot study N = 62 (30 Colombia, 29 Perú, 3 indicated Other country) was run to obtain reference values in dimensions relevant to social perception, which would help us to interpret possible effects.
Therefore, participants from both countries rated all target stimuli in likability, familiarity, competence and honesty.
Following Willis y Todorov (2006) approach, the mean trait judgments across participants served as the criterion judgments for the experiments.
text.formatted: Following Willis y <ref type="bibr">Todorov (2006)</ref> approach, the mean trait judgments across participants served as the criterion judgments for the experiments.

text.text: A semirandom selection of faces were applied, so each participant was exposed to a subset of 20 faces: 50% faces Colombia, 50% faces Peru; 50% 33ms, 50% 100ms.
Half of those 20 trials were rated on honesty and the other half on competence.
Therefore, the experimental task consists of 20 trials.
Participants were asked to respond quickly, using their first instinct.
Each trial started with a 500ms fixation cross.

Then, a target's face appeared on the screen (for 33ms or 100ms) followed by a 7-point likert scale of honesty or competence, which was available for 6s (1: dishonesty, 7: honesty; 1: incompetence; 7: competence, respectively) thus functioning as a backward mask.
Exposure times were selected based on previous research on face evaluation (Todorov et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Exposure times were selected based on previous research on face evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Todorov et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Response times for evaluative judgments were measured.
Once the scale disappeared, participants were asked if they recognized the target face through a yes/no recognition judgment.
The interval between trials was1500ms.
Once they had completed the 20 speeded trials, participants saw the same 20 faces again, one at a time, in a newly randomized order and without time constraint.
For each face, they rated the likelihood of choosing that candidate for a public position on a 7-point Likert scale (How likely are you to vote for this person for public position?
1: not at all likely; 7: very likely).
Because the order of the voting block was reshuffled, the speeded rating and the vote of the same face were separated by a variable number of other faces.
The instructions for the speeded block did not announce the voting block, which was introduced only after the last speeded trial.
An awareness check was administered at the end of the session
Analyses were conducted in R using lme4 and lmerTest for linear mixedeffects models (LMMs) and emmeans for simple slopes and contrasts; data and analysis code are available on OSF.
All models included crossed random effects for participants and candidates, so that inferences generalize across both samples of people and of faces.

The random-effects structure began with a by-participant random slope for the impression and was simplified only when a model failed to converge or produced a singular fit; unless noted otherwise, the maximal structure was retained.

Categorical predictors were effect-coded (-0.5/+0.5): exposure time (33/100 ms), judgment type (competence/honesty), recognition (not recognized/recognized), candidate country, and participant country.
Impression ratings were z-standardized within judgment type, so that slopes express the change in voting intention (1-7) per 1 SD of that trait's impression and are directly comparable across traits.

Fixed effects are reported with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; simple slopes and contrasts use the asymptotic approximation, which at this number of trials is equivalent to Satterthwaite and computationally far cheaper.
Tests were two-tailed with α = .05.
Because judgment type varied between trials -each face was rated on one trait only -honesty and competence could not be entered as two predictors of the same vote.

The honesty-versus-competence comparison (RQ1) was therefore modelled as the difference between the two impression-vote slopes within a single mixed model, which respects the repeated-measures structure better than comparing two independent correlations; within-subject correlations are reported alongside as a descriptive reference.

Of 498 recruited participants, 14 were excluded following the preregistered criteria: nine provided fewer than 70% valid responses in the evaluative task, five showed zero variance in their evaluative responses, and none responded consistently faster than 200 ms.
At the trial level, 23 individual ratings (0.24% of nontimeout responses) with response times below 200 ms were discarded.
The final sample comprised N = 484 participants and 9,680 trials.

Analyses of voting intention were based on the 9,210 trials with both a valid impression rating and a valid vote rating (2,842 recognized, 6,368 unrecognized); analyses restricted to honesty trials were based on 4,614 trials.
Participants resided in Colombia (n = 199, 41.1%) or Peru (n = 285, 58.9%); 331 identified as women (68.4%), 146 as men (30.2%) and 7 as non-binary (1.4%).
Age was collected in bands, and 87.0% of the sample fell in the 18-25 band.
The median session lasted 3.6 min (IQR = 2.9-4.3).

At the end of the session participants reported how clearly they had seen the briefly presented faces: 7.9% reported seeing nothing at all, 37.8% a face they could not make out clearly, 39.9% several faces they could not make out clearly, and 14.5% several faces clearly.
The manipulation of suboptimal processing conditions was therefore effective for 85.5% of the sample.
Participants reported recognizing the candidate on 30.8% of trials.
Recognition depended jointly on exposure time and on whether the candidate was from the participant's own country (Table 1).

text.text: Facial appeal thus guided voting intentions when candidates were not identified, whereas reputation and prominence guided them when they were.

Given the null results for RQ1, RQ2a and RQ2b, we computed the smallest effect detectable with 80% power as approximately 2.8 times the observed standard error of each focal term.

The nulls for RQ1 and RQ2a are therefore informative, whereas the test of RQ2b was less conclusive.
Voting intentions were rated under free viewing, after the speeded block.

The impression-vote relation could therefore reflect information extracted during the brief exposure, impressions formed or revised while viewing the face freely, or a tendency to answer consistently with the earlier rating.

Re-estimating the models on person-mean-centred impressions left the exposure effect (b = 0.12, SE = 0.03, p < .001), the absence of awareness moderation (b = 0.05, p = .458) and the distance × recognition interaction (b = -0.10, SE = 0.04, p = .011) unchanged.

Taken together, these analyses suggest that the impression-vote relation is not simply a product of free viewing or of consistent responding: it depended on how long the face had been seen in the speeded phase, it did not depend on reported awareness, and for unrecognized candidates it did not weaken with the distance between rating and vote.
At the same time, part of the strong relation for recognized candidates appears to reflect carry-over of the earlier response or of the identification that accompanied it.
In addition, the evidence that impressions formed after only 33 ms predict voting intentions for unrecognized candidates is weak once between-participant differences in scale use are removed.
The clearest evidence for a contribution of the brief exposure therefore comes from the 100-ms condition.
None of the three preregistered dissociations emerged as predicted.
Instead, the results converge on two routes from facial appearance to voting intentions.

Impressions formed with as little as 33 ms of exposure predicted voting intentions even for candidates participants did not recognize, and on those trials the vote tracked the shared facial appeal of the candidate rather than any consensus about their honesty or competence.

When participants identified the candidate -and only when that candidate was from their own country -the impression-vote relation tripled and voting intentions tracked reputation and prominence instead of facial appeal.
Across both routes, longer exposure strengthened the impression-vote relation equally for honesty and competence.

Finally, agreement with free-viewing criterion judgments revealed the temporal dissociation that the vote-based tests did not: honesty impressions were aligned with the normative consensus after 33 ms, whereas competence impressions required 100 ms.
This study evaluates whether facial impressions of honesty and competence, formed under suboptimal processing conditions, predict voting intentions for actual political candidates.

By conducting this research within the electoral contexts of the 2026 presidential elections in Colombia and Peru, we capture a unique opportunity to examine the implicit components of electoral preference in authentic, high-stakes environments.

The findings demonstrate that facial impressions made under suboptimal conditions predict voting intentions, but this relationship is substantially moderated by candidate recognition and origin rather than holding uniformly.
Specifically, candidate familiarity strongly amplifies the impression-vote relation for own-country candidates, whereas for foreign candidates, the effect disappears or remains minimal.

Furthermore, because voting intentions were indicated during unconstrained free viewing following the speeded task, claims that impressions formed exclusively under suboptimal conditions drive voting decisions must be tempered; initial rapid cues interact with subsequent deliberate viewing during final choice.

These results refine established literature on the automaticity of trustworthiness and competence evaluations (Ballew & Todorov, 2007; Todorov et al., 2009; Willis & Todorov, 2006), reinforcing the evidence that voting behavior remains susceptible to rapid facial cues, particularly when integrated with familiar candidate representations (Banducci et al., 2008; Lenz & Lawson, 2011; Olivola & Todorov, 2010).

text.text: These findings could be interpreted as new evidence on the automaticity of appearance-based trait inferences in voting intentions.

Specifically, our results corroborate prior research demonstrating that voters implicitly derive perceptions of friendliness and competence from facial appearance to inform their voting intentions (Ballew & Todorov, 2007; Hall et al., 2009; Laustsen & Petersen, 2018; Rule et al., 2010; Todorov et al., 2005). Ballew and Todorov (2007) showed that impressions of competence could be formed as little as 100ms exposure to faces, without any deliberation, and that these impressions can influence voting decisions (see also, Olivola & Todorov, 2010).

text.text: Our results confirm and extend these findings, by showing that both competence and honesty impressions could be formed with as little as 33ms exposure to faces and that these impressions are predictive of voting intentions.

Unlike Ballew and Todorov (2007), who use software generated-faces, the use of faces of real political candidates in this research made it possible to show that rapid facial impressions are consistent with candidates preferences in more naturalistic settings.

text.text: Crucially, our findings demonstrate that facial impressions are most predictive of voting intentions when the candidate is familiar, revealing that recognition substantially moderates this relationship.

Our finding that familiarity amplified, rather than attenuated, the relationship between facial impressions and electoral choices contrasts with previous literature, which posits that such effects are amplified under conditions of low political knowledge or candidate unfamiliarity (Fiske, 2019; Unkelbach et al., 2023).

text.text: From a processing perspective, brief exposure durations (33-100 ms) followed by backward masking effectively interrupt ongoing visual input, limiting sensory processing to early feed-forward activity.
However, ultra-fast familiarity and identity processing can occur within these latencies (Wiese et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, ultra-fast familiarity and identity processing can occur within these latencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Wiese et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In this rapid window, a familiar face may act as an instantaneous retrieval key that reactivates pre-existing cognitive and emotional political attitudes.
These entrenched attitudes are structured not only by deliberative knowledge but by peripheral associations accessible immediately upon identity retrieval (Lau & Redlawsk, 2001).
text.formatted: These entrenched attitudes are structured not only by deliberative knowledge but by peripheral associations accessible immediately upon identity retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Lau & Redlawsk, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, when participants subsequently rate voting intentions under free-viewing conditions, these reactivated attitudes may help shape and reinforce the initial impression-vote link for own-country candidates, whereas unrecognized foreign candidates lack this attitude-retrieval mechanism Regarding our second hypothesis, the results contradict the expectation that honesty impressions would demonstrate a stronger correlation with voting intentions than competence.

Unlike previous research suggesting a clear moral primacywhere morality-related judgments dominate impression formation (Brambilla et al., 2012; Leach et al., 2007)-our findings reveal that both honesty and competence are equally predictive of electoral preferences.

text.text: This parity suggests that the moral primacy hypothesis may be less rigid within the political domain.

While morality is undoubtedly a core pillar of social evaluation, competence remains a central predictor of voting behavior, likely reflecting an 'adaptive followership' mechanism where voters seek cues indicative of problem-solving efficacy (Laustsen & Petersen, 2018).

text.text: Our findings align with more recent applications of the Stereotype Content Model (Fiske, 2019), which emphasizes the nuanced, parallel roles of these dimensions in shaping political perception.

text.text: Regarding our third hypotheses, our findings indicate that both honesty and competence impressions form rapidly-within 33 ms-suggesting that the underlying psychological mechanisms are highly efficient.

Although we did not observe the predicted temporal dissociation in the impression-vote relationship, a clear dissociation emerged at the level of information extraction: honesty impressions aligned with criterion judgments at 33 ms, whereas competence impressions required additional processing time.
This delay suggests that competence evaluations at 33 ms may initially rely on valence-based processing before stabilizing into distinct competence-related judgments at 100 ms.
Our results suggest that the identity-vote association is a more stable phenomenon than the honesty-vote association, which appears sensitive to the duration of exposure.

This may reflect the cognitive architecture of these judgments: identity recognition functions as a retrieval process in which pre-existing attitudes are activated once a familiarity threshold is reached, rendering the association relatively invariant to short-term exposure fluctuations (Dobs et al., 2019).

text.text: Conversely, honesty judgments-even under suboptimal conditions-may involve a more constructive, evaluative process that benefits from, and is therefore moderated by, the incremental processing time available between 33 ms and 100 ms.
Despite the contributions, the present study is not free of limitations.

First, by utilizing real photographs of political candidates, we introduced a methodological trade-off: we prioritized the ecological validity of the research over the use of a standardized set of face stimuli.
Although a pilot study was conducted to mitigate potential biases, we could not control all facial features that influence electoral perception.
For instance, dimensions such as perceived age and face typicality were not systematically assessed.

Regarding age, findings in the literature remain contradictory: Zebrowitz and Montepare (2005) suggested that the positive effect of perceived competence on election outcomes may be mediated by perceived age, noting that 'baby-faced' politicians are less likely to be elected than their more mature-faced counterparts.

text.text: Conversely, Olivola and Todorov (2010) found that a baby-faced appearance was a positive predictor of both actual and hypothetical votes.

text.text: Future studies should address the role of perceived age and face typicality/resemblance in the obtained findings.

Second, a key methodological limit involves the measurement of voting intentions: because voting likelihood was rated during unconstrained free viewing immediately following the speeded evaluation task, our paradigm cannot claim that voting decisions are driven exclusively by suboptimal viewing conditions.

Additional analyses of the voting measure indicate that while brief exposure effects carried over to voting decisions (particularly at 100 ms), post-exposure free viewing and response consistency-especially for recognized candidates-interact with these initial rapid cues.
Future research should utilize paradigms that constrain both the trait rating and the voting decision under identical time limitations to further isolate pure implicit effects.
The present findings demonstrate that electoral preferences are anchored in early, heuristic-driven information processing, often occurring before voters consciously identify candidates.

When the candidate is unknown, these initial impressions may establish a foundational anchoring bias, which likely shapes subsequent information processing, risking a confirmation bias (Kahneman, 2011) as voters interpret later candidate messaging through the lens of their first impressions.

text.text: While these initial impressions are potent, they are not deterministic.

Voting decisions are multi-faceted processes shaped by a confluence of variables, including political affiliation, ideology, and candidate proposals, that can mitigate or override initial facial evaluations (Ahler et al., 2017; Hayes et al., 2014; Jenke & Huettel, 2020).

text.text: Consequently, campaign strategists must be cognizant of the temporal dynamics of these biases to develop more effective communication interventions.
Campaign assessors should first identify the specific social dimensions triggered by a candidate's appearance to optimize persuasion strategies.
When candidates face negative impressions of competence, communication should leverage multimodal consistency.

Because leadership and competence are frequently inferred from vocal characteristics, such as verbal fluency, moderate pacing, and prosodic confidence (Klofstad et al., 2012; 2016), campaigns can utilize these cues to update initial impressions.

text.text: Furthermore, formats such as structured debates and long-form interviews are essential to trigger a shift from automatic to deliberative processing.
By employing both peripheral and central persuasive cues (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986), candidates can disrupt initial heuristics.

text.text: Strategies should include presenting verifiable track records, professional attire, and clear policy messaging.
Conversely, negative impressions regarding honesty pose a greater hurdle.
While vocal acoustics can modulate these perceptions, such effects are highly context-dependent, precluding a standardized 'ideal' speech pattern (Maltezou-Papastylianou et al., 2025).

text.text: Furthermore, because trustworthiness evaluations are largely resistant to rapid, peripheral persuasion, mitigating these biases necessitates long-term strategies that emphasize transparency, behavioral consistency, and authentic discourse to foster an enduring perception of integrity (Grimmelikhuijsen & Meijer, 2014).

text.text: In conclusion, this research demonstrates that facial impressions of honesty and competence, formed under suboptimal processing conditions predict voting intentions for actual political candidates through an integrated process heavily moderated by candidate recognition.

Rather than operating uniformly across all targets, rapid facial cues trigger an amplified predictive pathway specifically when candidates are recognized from one's own country, as ultra-fast identity processing (Wiese et al., 2024) allows the familiar face to serve as an instantaneous retrieval key for pre-existing political attitudes.
text.formatted: Rather than operating uniformly across all targets, rapid facial cues trigger an amplified predictive pathway specifically when candidates are recognized from one's own country, as ultra-fast identity processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Wiese et al., 2024)</ref> allows the familiar face to serve as an instantaneous retrieval key for pre-existing political attitudes.

text.text: Conversely, for foreign candidates, this relation is minimal or absent.
Moreover, because final voting choices were evaluated during unconstrained free viewing, these initial speeded impressions inform rather than fully replace subsequent deliberate processing.

By utilizing real political candidates within Colombian and Peruvian electoral contexts, this study underscores that rapid face perception interacts dynamically with pre-existing cognitive structures in naturalistic political decision-making.
